topics.title: Meaning and Objective of Receivables Management
explain: Receivables management involves planning and controlling debts owed to a firm from credit sales.
It is also known as trade credit management.
The core objective is to optimize the return on investment in receivables.
High investment in receivables increases collection costs and bad debt risks.
Low investment restricts sales volume because competitors may offer more liberal credit terms.

flow.title: Trade Credit Management Cycle
steps: Sell goods to customers on credit terms
Record debt balance under accounts receivable
Block funds in debtors as working capital
Execute collection efforts to recover dues
Optimize overall return on debtor investment

topics.example: A wholesale dealer grants 30-day credit to retailers to boost sales while keeping enough liquidity to restock inventory.
remember: The primary objective is optimizing return on investment in receivables, not just maximizing sales.
mistakes: Assuming that minimizing receivables to zero is ideal without considering lost sales opportunities.

quiz.q: What is another common name for management of receivables?
quiz.why: Management of receivables refers to trade credit extended to customers, so it is also called trade credit management.

quiz.q: What risk arises if a firm maintains a very low investment in receivables?
o: Restricted sales due to rigid terms
quiz.why: Low investment in receivables means strict credit terms, which can restrict sales if competitors offer liberal terms.

topics.title: Aspects of Management of Debtors
explain: Credit Policy: Establishes credit standards, terms, cash discount policies, and collection efforts.
Credit Analysis: Evaluates customer risk and creditworthiness before approving credit.
Control of Receivables: Executes credit policies and follows up with defaulting debtors.
Credit terms like '3/15 net 60' mean a 3% discount if paid in 15 days; otherwise full payment in 60 days.
Costs of maintaining receivables include carrying (interest/opportunity) cost, administrative cost, collection cost, and default cost.

flow.title: Debtor Management Framework
steps: Formulate balanced credit standards and terms
Perform credit analysis on prospective buyers
Grant credit with defined discount periods
Monitor outstanding balances and collection efforts
Manage carrying, administrative, and default costs

topics.example: A seller offers '2/10 net 45', giving buyers a 2% discount if paid within 10 days, or net payment due in 45 days.
remember: Carrying cost is based on interest or opportunity cost of funds blocked in debtors.
mistakes: Confusing the cash discount period with the net credit period in credit terms such as '3/15 net 60'.

quiz.q: In the credit term '3/15 net 60', what does '3/15' represent?
quiz.why: 3/15 indicates a 3% cash discount is granted if payment is settled within 15 days.

quiz.q: Which cost occurs because capital is locked up in receivables rather than earning interest elsewhere?
quiz.why: Funds tied up in receivables involve an opportunity cost equal to the interest or return lost elsewhere.

topics.title: Factors Determining Credit Policy
explain: Credit policy determines both the quantity and quality of accounts receivable.
Factors include sales volume impact, credit terms, cash discount rate, and selection practices.
Customer paying habits and the firm's collection practices directly impact investment size.
Operating efficiency in billing and record keeping reduces administration costs.
A lenient policy sells liberally to boost sales; a stringent policy limits credit to creditworthy buyers.

flow.title: Credit Policy Determination
steps: Assess impact of credit on sales volume
Define credit terms and discount incentives
Set selection standards for credit buyers
Analyze customer payment practices and habits
Improve efficiency in billing and collection

topics.example: A company facing tough competition eases its credit terms from 30 days to 50 days to attract more buyers.
remember: A rising trend in collection and billing costs depresses the size of investment in receivables.
mistakes: Assuming a lenient credit policy always leads to higher net profit without checking bad debt losses.

quiz.q: Which policy approach sells on credit only to selective customers with high creditworthiness?
quiz.why: A stringent credit policy restricts sales on credit strictly to highly creditworthy and sound buyers.

quiz.q: How do rising collection costs and bad debt losses affect the size of investment in receivables?
o: They double the cash discount rate
They have no impact on working capital
quiz.why: Higher operational costs and losses depress the profitable investment size in receivables.

topics.title: Factors Under the Control of the Finance Manager
explain: The finance manager holds operating responsibility for managing investment in receivables.
Key duties include supervising credit administration and setting credit application selection criteria.
Contributes to top management decisions on optimal credit policies.
Speeds up conversion of receivables into cash through aggressive collection policies.
Must balance the cost of increased investment in receivables against profits from higher sales.

flow.title: Finance Manager Responsibilities
steps: Supervise day-to-day administration of credit
Formulate application selection criteria for buyers
Advise management on best credit policy
Implement aggressive collection for faster cash conversion
Balance carrying costs against additional sales profits

topics.example: A finance manager sets strict credit score thresholds for new buyers to prevent bad debts while maintaining growth.
remember: The core duty is balancing additional carrying costs against incremental sales profits.
mistakes: Believing the finance manager is only responsible for collection and not policy formulation.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a direct responsibility of the finance manager in receivable management?
o: Deciding criteria for selection of credit applications
quiz.why: Deciding criteria for selecting credit applications is an operational role of the finance manager.

quiz.q: What is the primary balance a finance manager must strike in receivable management?
o: Variable costs vs fixed overhead costs
Cost of increased receivables investment vs sales profits
Tax expense vs debt interest payments
quiz.why: The manager balances the cost of holding more receivables against profits generated by higher credit sales.

topics.title: Approaches to Evaluation of Credit Policies
explain: Two main methods exist for evaluating proposed credit policies: Total Approach and Incremental Approach.
Total Approach compares total expected profits after tax and opportunity costs across all policy options.
Incremental Approach evaluates incremental expected profits against required return on incremental investment.
Opportunity Cost = Total Cost of Credit Sales × (Collection Period / 365 or 360) × Required Return Rate.
Total Fixed Cost = (Average Cost per unit - Variable Cost per unit) × Units sold under present policy.

flow.title: Credit Policy Evaluation Steps
steps: Estimate credit sales under proposed policies
Deduct variable costs, fixed costs, and bad debts
Subtract cash discounts to obtain net profit
Calculate opportunity cost of blocked capital
Select policy with highest net benefit

topics.example: A firm compares keeping a 30-day terms policy versus switching to 40-day terms by calculating extra profit against extra carrying cost.
remember: Opportunity cost is calculated on Total Cost of Credit Sales, not on Credit Sales value.
mistakes: Using Credit Sales instead of Total Cost as the base for calculating opportunity cost.

quiz.q: Under standard evaluation of credit policies, opportunity cost of receivables is calculated on which base?
quiz.why: Opportunity cost reflects capital blocked, which is measured by Total Cost of Credit Sales.

quiz.q: How is Net Benefit calculated under the Total Approach?
o: Expected Profit after Tax minus Opportunity Cost of Receivables
Total Fixed Costs minus Collection Costs
quiz.why: Net Benefit equals Expected Profit after Tax (A) minus Opportunity Cost of Investment in Receivables (B).

topics.title: Financing Receivables - Pledging and Factoring
explain: Pledging: Using receivables as collateral for a short-term loan (lender finances around 50% to 90%). It increases borrowing and debt-equity ratio.
Factoring: Outright sale of receivables to a financial agency (factor) for immediate cash.
Recourse Factoring: If debtors default, the factor recovers the loss from the client firm.
Non-Recourse Factoring: The factor bears the loss of bad debts and charges a higher commission.
Factoring provides immediate liquidity without creating a net financial liability on the balance sheet.

flow.title: Factoring Mechanism Flow
steps: Firm sells goods on credit to customer
Firm sells invoices to factor agency
Factor advances cash minus reserve and commission
Customer pays factor directly on due date
Factor releases remaining reserve balance to firm

topics.example: A firm sells ₹30 lakh receivables to a factor, receives an immediate advance of 80%, and avoids maintaining a collection department.
remember: Factoring does not create debt liability on the balance sheet like pledged loans do.
mistakes: Assuming pledged receivables are removed from the balance sheet.

quiz.q: Who bears the risk of bad debts in a non-recourse factoring agreement?
quiz.why: In non-recourse factoring, the factor assumes the ultimate risk of loss from debtor defaults.

quiz.q: What is a main disadvantage of pledging accounts receivables for short-term loans?
o: It increases debt and impacts debt-equity ratio
It forces the sale of fixed assets
quiz.why: Pledging is a loan, so it increases total debt on the balance sheet and affects leverage ratios.

topics.title: Forfaiting
explain: Forfaiting comes from the French term 'forfait' meaning 'relinquish a right'.
It is a non-recourse bill discounting facility used specifically for export trade.
Financial institutions/banks buy trade bills/invoices from exporters without recourse.
Importers obtain goods on deferred payment terms by opening Letters of Credit.
EXIM Bank of India's 'Buyer's Credit' is an example of a forfaiting arrangement.

flow.title: Forfaiting Process Steps
steps: Exporter sells goods to overseas importer
Importer draws Letter of Credit via Importer Bank
Exporter presents LC/bills to Exporter Bank
Exporter Bank buys bills on non-recourse basis
Exporter receives immediate payment without recourse risk

topics.example: An Indian exporter sells machinery to a German buyer on 2-year credit; a forfaiter buys the bills, paying the exporter cash upfront.
remember: Forfaiting is always on a non-recourse basis for international export trade.
mistakes: Confusing domestic recourse factoring with export forfaiting.

quiz.q: What does the French word 'Forfait' mean in forfaiting?
quiz.why: 'Forfait' literally translates to 'relinquish a right' to future receivables.

quiz.q: Which Indian institution provides Buyer's Credit as a forfaiting facility?
quiz.why: EXIM Bank of India offers Buyer's Credit as a forfaiting mechanism for Indian exporters.

topics.title: Innovations in Receivable Management
explain: Re-engineering: Fundamental redesign of processes, centralizing high-value receivables for efficiency.
Alternative Payment Modes: Direct debit, IVR (phone payments), Lock Box processing, and electronic methods (RTGS, NEFT, UPI).
Lock Box Processing: Outsourced partner collects cheques and data, transmitting files to the client firm.
Use of Technology: Automated Accounts Receivable Management Systems update sales, inventory, and ledger records instantly.
Decision Tree Analysis: Evaluates credit granting decisions using probability distributions of customer payment and default.

flow.title: Modern Receivable Processing Steps
steps: Centralize high-value customer accounts
Provide digital payment options like UPI and IVR
Use Lock Box processing for fast cheque clearing
Automate ledger updates using integrated software
Apply Decision Tree Analysis for risky credit approvals

topics.example: A firm uses Lock Box processing where a bank opens customer mail, deposits cheques immediately, and sends data electronically.
remember: Decision tree analysis calculates weighted net benefit based on recovery and default probabilities.
mistakes: Thinking Lock Box processing is a credit scoring model rather than a remittance collection system.

quiz.q: What is Lock Box Processing in receivable management?
o: A physical vault for storing cash
An outsourced system capturing cheques/invoices to speed up funds availability
A penalty clause for late paying customers
quiz.why: Lock box processing outsources cheque and invoice collection to accelerate cash processing.

quiz.q: Which tool evaluates credit granting by calculating expected monetary values from payment probabilities?
quiz.why: Decision tree analysis uses payment and non-payment probabilities to compute weighted net benefit of granting credit.

topics.title: Monitoring of Receivables
explain: Monitoring is essential to check if receivable management policies are effective.
Average Collection Period measures the average age of outstanding receivables.
Ageing Schedule classifies debtors into age brackets (e.g., 1-30 days, 31-60 days, 61-90 days, etc.).
Ageing schedule highlights accumulation of old overdue accounts for timely action.
Debt Collection Programme steps: Intimations before due date, reminders on due date, legal escalation reminders, legal action.
Collection spending reaches a saturation point beyond which further expenditure yields minimal reduction in bad debts.

flow.title: Debtor Monitoring and Collection Flow
steps: Compute average collection period
Prepare Ageing Schedule categorizing debtor balances
Send pre-due date intimations and reminders
Follow escalation matrix for overdue accounts
Initiate legal recourse for uncollectible debts

topics.example: An ageing schedule reveals that 53% of balances are over 60 days old, prompting management to send urgent collection notices.
remember: Beyond the saturation point, extra collection expenses have negligible impact on bad debt losses.
mistakes: Assuming collection expenses should be increased indefinitely without checking the saturation point.

quiz.q: What is the primary function of an Ageing Schedule of receivables?
o: To categorize receivables by age brackets to monitor quality
quiz.why: An Ageing Schedule groups debtors by age categories to identify old, uncollected balances.

quiz.q: What happens when collection expenses are increased beyond the saturation point?
o: Bad debts immediately drop to zero
Cost increases with negligible additional impact on bad debts
quiz.why: At the saturation point, further collection expenditure yields very little additional reduction in bad debts.
